vignette:
He is fifty-four now, a married Latin American man who built his life around work, family, and the steady belief that if something is broken, a person should show up and help fix it. Before the war zone, he runs a small but growing business and is known as the kind of owner who remembers employees’ children’s names, stays late to solve problems, and takes pride in being dependable. When a humanitarian organization asks for experienced Spanish-speaking volunteers to help coordinate supply distribution in a conflict area, he tells himself he can be useful. He speaks about it, even now, as a practical decision at first. People need food, medicine, transport. He knows logistics. He knows how to stay calm.

In the early days there, he moves on adrenaline and purpose. He helps unload trucks, organize routes, and negotiate with frightened civilians and armed young men at checkpoints. The work feels urgent and clean in a moral sense. He sleeps little, drinks bad coffee, and keeps going. Then the violence gets closer. He hears shelling often enough that his body begins to anticipate it before his mind does. One afternoon, while helping move families into what they are told is a safer building, an explosion hits nearby. The force throws him to the ground. Dust fills his mouth. He cannot hear for several seconds except for a piercing ring. When the sound returns, it comes all at once—screaming, metal, someone shouting for a child.

He remembers seeing a mother with blood on her face trying to lift concrete with her bare hands. He remembers his own hands shaking so hard he cannot get a bandage open. Most of all he remembers a boy, about the age his youngest son had been years earlier, lying still in a hallway with one sneaker missing. He had seen suffering before in news footage and in difficult neighborhoods at home, but the intimacy of that moment undoes something in him. Afterward he keeps working because there is no room not to. In the following weeks he moves through destroyed streets carrying boxes of antibiotics and bottled water while scanning rooftops, flinching at engines backfiring, feeling anger toward anyone who tells him to rest. At night he lies down fully clothed, boots on, waiting.

When he comes home, everyone expects relief. His wife cries at the airport and holds his face in both hands. Friends call him brave. At first he tries to fit himself back into ordinary life. He returns to the business, walks the warehouse floor, reviews invoices, sits in meetings. But he startles when a pallet drops. A delivery truck’s air brakes make his chest lock up. He begins checking exits in restaurants, then stops going to restaurants at all. Fireworks send him straight to the floor before he understands where he is. He tells people he is tired, overworked, jet-lagged, though months pass.

Sleep becomes the place he dreads most. He wakes choking on dust that is not there, convinced for several seconds that the bedroom ceiling is collapsing. His wife learns not to touch him suddenly from behind. Once, when she tries to wake him from a nightmare, he swings his arm hard enough to bruise her shoulder. He is horrified afterward and apologizes over and over, but shame settles in him. He starts sleeping on the couch some nights, claiming he does not want to disturb her. He does not tell her that in his dreams he is back in that hallway, unable to reach the boy, unable to hear anything but the ringing.

During the day he becomes harder, less recognizable to himself. At work he used to mentor employees patiently; now he snaps at small mistakes and cannot tolerate delays. He stares at spreadsheets and realizes he has read the same line ten times. He avoids the news but also feels compelled to monitor every conflict update, as if vigilance might prevent another catastrophe somewhere. He keeps extra bottled water, batteries, and medical supplies in his car. When his adult children are late answering texts, he imagines bodies under rubble before he imagines traffic.

His wife tells him he is home physically but not really with her. He knows she is right. Family gatherings feel unbearably loud. Music, laughter, clattering plates—ordinary joy presses on him like threat. Sometimes, in the middle of a birthday party or a busy workday, an image cuts across his mind with cinematic clarity: the mother’s bloody hands, the boy’s bare sock, the gray dust coating everyone’s hair. In those moments the present disappears. He smells smoke that no one else smells. His heart races and his skin goes cold. He steps outside, breathing hard, ashamed that he cannot master his own body.

What troubles him almost as much as the fear is the guilt. He has money, a home, grandchildren on the way, a wife who still reaches for him in the dark. Other people did not leave. He tells himself he has no right to complain, no right to be haunted when others are dead. Yet his world has narrowed around avoidance and alertness. He delegates more of the business because he cannot manage crowds, noise, or uncertainty the way he once could. He still gets up early, still puts on the face of a capable owner and provider, but underneath he feels perpetually braced, as if another blast is always seconds away.
